title: Longest Walk in a Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Treat each parent–child link as a path you can walk in either direction. Return the length of the longest walk between any two nodes, counted in edges, never visiting a node twice.

The longest walk does not have to pass through the root.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.in: root = [9, 4, null, 3, 6, 2, null, null, 7, 1, null, null, 8]
examples.why: The walk 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 6 → 7 → 8 bends at 4 and never touches the root. Any walk through 9 is at most 4 edges, because 9 has nothing on its right.
A walk from the only node to itself has no edges.
1 → 3 → 5 → 8 → 9 passes five nodes but only four edges.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Every walk has one highest node, where it bends (or ends). If you fix that bending node, what is the longest walk through it?

Through node X the best walk goes as deep as possible into the left subtree and as deep as possible into the right one: height(left) + height(right) edges. Computing heights from scratch at every node repeats a lot of work.
Write one recursive height function. Before returning 1 + max(l, r), use the same l and r to update a best answer kept outside: best = max(best, l + r).

explain.intuition:
Picture any walk in the tree and find its highest node, the place where it turns from going up to going down. The walk is then a path down into that node's left subtree plus a path down into its right subtree. To make it as long as possible, go as deep as you can on each side. So the longest walk that bends at X has height(X.left) + height(X.right) edges, where height counts nodes on the longest downward path (0 for an empty side). The answer is the best of that over every node, not just the root.

The trick that makes it one pass: a height function already visits every node and already has l and r in hand right before it returns. So it can do two jobs at once. It returns the height, which its parent needs, and on the side it updates a shared best with l + r, which only the final answer needs. This "return one thing, record another" shape comes back in many tree problems.
steps: Keep a variable best = 0 outside the recursion.
Update best = max(best, l + r): the longest walk bending at this node.
Return 1 + max(l, r) to the parent. After calling height(root), return best.
pitfalls: Only measuring at the root: height(left) + height(right) of the root. The first example has its longest walk entirely inside the left subtree.
Counting nodes instead of edges. With height measured in nodes, l + r is already the edge count of the walk through the node; adding 1 is off by one.
Returning l + r to the parent instead of 1 + max(l, r). A parent can extend only one branch of a walk, not both.

solutions.title: Measure heights again at every node
solutions.idea: For each node, compute the heights of its two subtrees from scratch and try their sum. Correct, but nodes deep in the tree get re-measured once per ancestor.

solutions.title: Return height, record the best on the side
solutions.idea: One post-order pass. Each call returns its height to the parent and, before returning, updates the best walk that bends at this node.

followups: Return the walk itself (the list of node values), not just its length.
